item.title: Wordfence Argus Finds Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Upload Vulnerability in Gravity Forms
item.description:
CVE-2026-19513 (CVSS 8.1): Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in Gravity Forms affects 1M+ WordPress installs, enabling remote code execution on NGINX-backed sites.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-19513, CVSS 8.1 High. Gravity Forms versions up to and including 3.0.2 allow unauthenticated attackers to write a PNG/PHP polyglot to the plugin's public temp upload directory with an attacker-chosen .php extension. The root cause is a cryptographic domain-confusion flaw: wp_hash() was reused without context separation for both public form state and chunk-continuation auth, letting attackers reuse a legitimate URL hash to authenticate a malicious upload continuation request.
- Exploitation requires a public form with a multi-file upload field enabled. PNG and PDF are permitted by default, so no admin allowlist change is needed. The attacker supplies a benign carrier filename (safe.png) while forcing the sanitized temp destination to end in .php, then triggers a final-chunk rename that strips the .part suffix and leaves an executable file on disk.
- Impact is server-dependent. Apache installs are partially mitigated by a .htaccess the plugin writes to the upload directory, blocking PHP execution. NGINX ignores .htaccess, making RCE directly reachable. Even on protected Apache installs, writing a .html file enables stored same-origin XSS.

item.title: 5 Million WordPress Sites Affected by SQL Injection Vulnerability in All-in-One WP Migration and Backup WordPress Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-19949 (CVSS 8.8): Unauthenticated second-order SQL injection in All-in-One WP Migration and Backup affects 5 million WordPress sites, enabling full RCE with no credentials required.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-19949, CVSS 8.8 High. All versions up to and including 7.109 are vulnerable. Patch is version 7.110, released August 20, 2026. Update immediately.
- Attack chain is multi-step but requires zero authentication. Attacker plants malicious payloads via WordPress trackback pings (no login needed), then waits for an admin to run a normal export/import cycle. The replace_table_values() regex in Ai1wm_Database mishandles backslash runs at string boundaries, promoting stored comment data into live SQL during restore.
- The first injected row times out the restore pass, forcing a transaction commit that writes the real ai1wm_secret_key back to the options table. The second row reads that key and writes it to a publicly approved comment, leaking it via the unauthenticated REST comments endpoint.
- With the secret key in hand, the attacker drives the import action directly, uploading a crafted .wpress archive containing a malicious must-use plugin dropped to wp-content/mu-plugins and executed on next page load. Full RCE as the web server user.
Takeaway: Check your wp_comments table for trackbacks with trailing backslashes in comment_author or suspicious URLs in comment_author_url. Audit mu-plugins for unexpected files. Update to 7.110 now.

item.title: SLEEPWALKER: Passive Backdoor Awakens Only When Attackers Call
item.description:
SLEEPWALKER is a passive Windows backdoor that never beacons home, staying silent until a specially crafted packet wakes it, making traditional C2 detection nearly useless against it.
Key findings:
- SLEEPWALKER abuses DLL side-loading into ERAAgent.exe, the ESET Management Agent process, a trusted security tool turned into a hiding place. Any host running ESET endpoint management is a potential target worth checking for unexpected DLLs in the agent's directory.
- No fixed C2, no autonomous beaconing. The implant stays dormant until it receives a trigger packet, then decrypts and executes attacker-supplied bytecode in memory. This deliberately breaks network-based C2 detection that relies on periodic outbound connections.
- The custom 23-instruction command language supports scheduling, multiple comms mechanisms, staged payload delivery, lateral movement, and in-memory code execution. Attackers carry all logic in the packet, not in the implant, minimizing on-disk footprint.
- DFIR artifact focus: look for unsigned or unexpected DLLs loaded by ERAAgent.exe, suspicious inbound network packets to agent ports, and anomalous memory regions in that process. Prefetch, Sysmon Event ID 7 (ImageLoad), and process memory dumps are your starting points.
Hunt for DLL side-loading into ERAAgent.exe using Sysmon ImageLoad events filtered to unsigned modules. Memory forensics on that process is essential. Full IOC list available in the report.

item.title: Can AI Create PLC Attacks? Yes, But It’s Not That Easy Yet
item.description:
AI-assisted exploit porting achieved working RCE on a WAGO 750-831 PLC via CVE-2021-31886, requiring no authentication and executing arbitrary ARM shellcode, but cost $535 in API calls and bricked the device during C2 development.
Key findings:
- CVE-2021-31886 is a pre-auth buffer overflow in the Nucleus FTP server's USER command handler. Forescout used Claude Opus 4.6 with Ghidra and AI-generated Python scripts to port a working RCE from a WAGO 750-852 to a WAGO 750-831 running firmware V01.04.16, targeting 192.168.2[.]14 in the lab. The exploit sends ICMP and UDP beacons from the PLC with no credentials required on port 21.
- The critical technical hurdle was shellcode survival: normal FTP command processing zeroed the 256-byte buffer after the USER command, destroying the payload. The fix was a USER then CWD sequence without a CRLF terminator, bypassing the completion path that cleared the buffer and keeping attacker-controlled memory intact long enough for execution.
- Claude also independently flagged a separate potential buffer overflow in the FTP command extraction loop, distinct from CVE-2021-31886, now under separate investigation.
- Attempting to extend the RCE into a C2 implant bricked the physical PLC when a payload wrote to flash-mapped memory, illustrating that AI agents acting on cyber-physical systems can cause irreversible hardware damage.

item.title: China-Linked Fire Ant Turned Cisco Routers, TACACS Servers Into Espionage Platforms
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage group Fire Ant implanted Cisco IOS XR routers and TACACS servers with custom malware to harvest credentials, capture traffic, and erase forensic evidence, per Sygnia incident response findings.
- Fire Ant (assessed strong overlap with UNC3886, distinct from Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon) deployed control-plane malware on Cisco IOS XR routers and created GRE tunnel interfaces that left zero trace in device config files. On Linux jump hosts, BridgeAgent masqueraded as a Zabbix monitoring agent, persisting via a systemd unit. Both represent novel tooling, not reused implants.
- A previously unreported toolkit named TacTap injected a malicious library into the tac_plus daemon to intercept administrator credentials at authentication time, storing them with simple XOR obfuscation. Owning the authentication layer means every admin action was visible to the attacker.
- Anti-forensic work was systematic: syslog functions were patched to filter and delete selected records, wtmp and utmp entries were rewritten, SELinux was disabled, and firewall rules were altered. Backdoors triggered on magic strings inside network packets rather than listening ports, leaving port-based detection blind.
- Some components had lain dormant since 2025. Critical infrastructure networks were reached but activity appears limited to reconnaissance, consistent with long-term espionage positioning.

item.title: The Crypto Wallet That Never Opened: Tampered Exodus Installer Hides a Modular RAT
item.description:
A tampered Exodus Wallet installer delivered a six-module, memory-resident RAT to four organizations in under 90 minutes, using Azure Table Storage as a dead drop and never once showing a window to the victim.
- Four Huntress-protected orgs hit between late July and Aug 18 2026, three within 85 minutes of each other. Initial access came via .pdf.js double-extension lures (chrome.exe as parent), a ZIP-staged .js file, and an unused search-ms: WebDAV path on 35[.]212.159[.]20 / us05[.]org. The MSI (SHA256: c513a7346484ee69a2931c4a89956ee50aa63e4366ef989315e669d8f10d7485, 0/76 on VirusTotal) installs to %APPDATA%\ExdBackupTool\, bypassing UAC entirely.
- Three files inside app.asar were modified: exodus_patch.js overwrites BrowserWindow.show(), focus(), and center() so the wallet runs silently forever; keystokeage.js (50 MB) hides a PE32+ loader using koffi FFI calls to VirtualAlloc, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateThread. The 10 MB payload (SHA256: 8c3b41ea5a85778145a6e5772bfee2eb0f8b027d0af199fb71a76dfb8bb29e5a) is AES-256-CBC encrypted inline, never touches disk, and loads six plugin DLLs: dll4_cmd, dll4_fileman, dll4_browser, dll4_socks, dll4_vnc, and dll4_script.
- C2 runs as an Azure Table Storage dead drop: lgapistorage123[.]table.core.windows.net, table ftable434, T_ rows for tasking, R_ rows for results, deleted after read. No attacker-owned domain in the network path.

item.title: North Korea-linked IT Workers Are Getting Hired Inside Western Companies
item.description:

Workers use stolen or fabricated identities, VPNs, and proxy services like Astrill and IPRoyal to pass hiring checks, complete onboarding, and perform real job duties while routing pay back to North Korea 🇰🇵. Traditional EDR and network controls largely miss this because there is nothing to block.

These artifacts only connect when reviewed together.
- Hardware tells the story in case two. A corporate laptop cycled through a GL.iNet travel router, a residential WiFi network, then a PiKVM device before settling on permanent ethernet, the classic laptop farm setup. Within an hour the worker was testing microphones. Minutes before a Zoom call, they hit ip[.]me to confirm their proxy was live.

item.title: EtherHiding Exposed: What Security Leaders Need to Know

The attacker rotates infrastructure for fractions of a cent per transaction. Blocking a single IP or domain does not sever access. item.title: Ungentlemanly behavior: Insights into a ransomware operation
item.description:
GOLD SHERWOOD's "Gentlemen" RaaS hit 683 victims in under a year, with sub-24-hour dwell times, BYOVD EDR killers, and a repeatable affiliate playbook analysts can now map precisely.
Key findings:
- Initial access relied on stolen or brute-forced VPN credentials (CVE-2024-55591 cited in third-party reporting against FortiGate) with no MFA. Within the first hour, actors established redundant VPN sessions from multiple foreign IPs, then moved laterally via RDP to file servers and domain controllers using valid domain credentials. Privilege escalation came fast: net1 localgroup, net group "domain admins", and direct account password resets secured domain admin access before defenders could respond.
- Tool staging landed in C:\PerfLogs, a low-scrutiny Windows directory. EDR killing used the custom GentleKiller suite (Watchdog, Javelin, G11 variants) plus Havoc and Xkpsm-Killer, all abusing vulnerable drivers (nogbc.sys, G11.sys, dmx.sys) via BYOVD. Windows Defender was neutered via Add-MpPreference exclusions and registry keys, and avkill.bat was pushed domain-wide via NETLOGON.
- Exfiltration favored Rclone (5 of 15 incidents), with adaptive pivots to Restic and MinIO Client within a single intrusion. Ransom notes drop as README-GENTLEMEN.txt; Go-based locker binaries follow naming patterns like G_<ext>_windows_amd64.exe with --superfast/--ultrafast flags.

item.title: China-linked Fire Ant Hides Inside Trusted Infrastructure
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage group Fire Ant hijacked Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS auth servers, and Linux jump hosts, surgically erasing evidence to pivot toward critical infrastructure through trusted network relationships.
Key findings:
- Fire Ant deployed purpose-built IOS XR implants, not generic Linux malware. One component masqueraded as a boot service and ran only during odd-numbered hours to evade scheduled audits. Another hooked the syslog function directly, silently dropping any log message not containing the string "Health," making the router's own audit trail selectively false.
- TACACS credential theft went beyond credential harvesting: Fire Ant injected a malicious library into the live authentication daemon, intercepting plaintext credentials from every legitimate admin login in real time, sitting inside the process that decides who to trust. XOR key 0xEF on captured credentials overlaps with previously documented UNC3886 tooling.
- On Linux hosts, backdoors posed as system services, one impersonating a SentinelOne agent, remaining active in memory after its on-disk file was deleted. A passive backdoor inspected raw traffic for a magic string before activating, leaving no listening port to find. Some implants had been dormant since 2025.
- Evidence was actively rewritten: wtmp, utmp, and btmp login records were edited to replace the router's real IP with an internal address, and sudo entries were stripped from system logs.

item.title: Hackers Are Probing PaperCut Servers, and 47% Still Have No Patch
item.description:
CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 chain enables pre-auth RCE on PaperCut servers, actively exploited in the wild. 47% of tracked installs have no patch available.
Key findings:
- Two-CVE chain: CVE-2026-81578 is an authorization bypass where PaperCut checks permissions on the displayed page, not the action performed, allowing unauthenticated config changes. CVE-2026-82078 then loads unsafe Java classes via database utilities, enabling arbitrary code execution. Huntress confirmed SYSTEM-level RCE by triggering pc-app.exe to spawn charmap.exe without credentials.
- Real-world attacks observed in two environments were brief recon runs, whoami, ver, and tasklist only, lasting under two minutes. No secondary malware or C2 observed yet. Treat this as pre-operational staging, not a clean bill of health.
- Key forensic artifact: attackers drop a malicious .class file into PaperCut's installation directory, delete Udydn.out and server.log to cover tracks, but the Derby database log at /data/internal/derby.log survives. Look for the string "jdbc:derby:memory:pwn" as a high-confidence IOC.
- Version 23 and earlier have no patch yet and represent roughly 47% of the ~2,500 Huntress-tracked installs. A confirmed attack already hit a version 24 server before its fix shipped.
Patch PaperCut NG immediately if on version 25. If on v23 or earlier, pull the Application Server off the public internet now.

item.title: PaperCut RCE Chain: CVE-2026-82078 Exploited
item.description:
PaperCut CVE-2026-82078 (CVSSv4 9.4) chained with auth bypass CVE-2026-81578 (CVSSv4 8.8) enables pre-auth RCE. PaperCut confirms active exploitation and customer incidents as of August 31, 2026.
- CVE-2026-81578 bypasses authentication on the PaperCut NG/MF web management interface, letting an unauthenticated attacker modify system configuration before access validation completes. That config change feeds directly into CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe dynamic class-loading flaw (CWE-470) in database connection utilities that instantiates attacker-controlled Java classes from the application classpath, resulting in arbitrary bytecode execution in the PaperCut server process. No credentials required.
- Huntress confirmed limited exploitation in two customer environments. Observed post-exploitation activity included base64-encoded discovery commands: whoami and ver. Ransomware deployment has not been confirmed, but the investigation is ongoing and the assessment may change.
- Hunt artifacts per PaperCut guidance: suspicious pc-app.exe child processes, missing or truncated server.log, strings jdbc:derby:memory:pwn;create=true or cafebabe (Java class magic bytes) in logs, unexpected five-character .class files in the server lib directory, and unexpected .cmd or .out files in the PaperCut data content directory. Attackers are cleaning up, so absence of indicators does not clear a host.
- Fixed versions: 24.1.10, 25.0.13, and 26.0.5 via Emergency Patch Release 2.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2094712604371406954

item.title: Mirage Kitten targeting aviation and FinTech sectors across the Middle East and Africa with a new malware set

C2 uses AES-256-GCM over Azure subdomains: plugplay.azurewebsites[.]net, visitfinancedentists[.]com, healthcomfsdpower[.]com.

item.title: Pouring Pints - Untappd for Android Analysis
item.description:
Untappd for Android leaves behind SQLite databases, compressed API cache, and push notification XML that together reconstruct a user's location history, identity, and check-in timeline.
Key findings:
- Two SQLite databases may exist under data/data/com.untappdllc.app/databases: clevertap (table: userProfiles, column: data) holds name, username, email, gender, date of birth as Unix seconds, and last checked-in beer. superwall_database (table: ManagedEventData) logs app_install, app_launch, app_close, and device_attributes events with epoch timestamps in milliseconds, approximate IP-derived location, OS version, app version, and network type.
- The cache folder at data/data/com.untappdllc.app/cache/http-cache stores gzip-compressed JSON files. Files with a .1 extension contain API responses including Discover page GPS coordinates, full check-in records with timestamps, beer and venue details, and Foursquare location suggestions. The paired .0 metadata file provides the timestamp when coordinates were loaded, filling the gap where the JSON itself carries no time value.
- Push notifications are preserved in shared_prefs/io.invertase.firebase.xml as JSON entries containing title, body, pushType, and a messageId embedding a Unix epoch timestamp. This can surface venue alerts, beer stock notifications, and social interactions even after the app UI is cleared.

item.description:
Guildma (Astaroth) banking malware delivered via geofenced Brazilian 🇧🇷 Portuguese 🇵🇹 phishing email, using ADS and AutoIt to establish persistence on Windows hosts.
Key findings:
- Initial access via a contract-themed email ("CONTRATO_ASSINATURA_DIGITAL") spoofing a DocuSign-style sender. The link hxxps://sistema-ekg3h4htc0h0ggdh.canadacentral-01.azurewebsites[.]net/ only delivers the payload if the victim uses a Brazil 🇧🇷 IP and Brazilian 🇧🇷 Portuguese 🇵🇹 locale settings, otherwise it serves a clean Android Studio installer as a decoy.

item.title: Breaking the Seal: Static Deobfuscation of JSCeal’s Compiled V8 Bytecode
item.description:
JSCeal crypto-stealer hides inside compiled V8 bytecode. Check Point Research built a fully static deobfuscation pipeline to crack it open without executing the malware, exposing keylogging, browser credential theft, and an HTTPS MITM proxy.
- JSCeal (also tagged WEEVILPROXY or MeadowLocust) arrives as app.jsc, a Brotli-compressed V8 code cache executed by a bundled Node.js runtime. Because the JavaScript was obfuscated with javascript-obfuscator before V8 compilation, analysts receive RC4-encrypted string chunks, control-flow flattening, proxy indirection, and operation wrappers on top of version-sensitive bytecode.

An optional LLM renaming stage (Claude or GPT) labels the resulting function graph. All 23 collected payloads produced analyzable output.

item.title: A KQL Query Is Not a Detection: What My Microsoft Sentinel Lab Actually Validated
item.description:
A compiled KQL query is not proof of detection: this Sentinel lab shows the full validation chain from raw telemetry through alert and incident, and reveals which rules earned that status.

AuditLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs each need their own Entra diagnostic setting routed to the workspace. Neither arrives by default, and a daily cap gap is not evidence of no activity.

- Rule 2 (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, same SessionId across 2+ IPs, T1550.001) and Rule 3 (cross-table join correlating auth then directory change within 30 min, T1098.001) remain disabled and unvalidated because the lab could not reproduce the exact trigger conditions in both native tables.
- The honest validation chain is: test action, raw telemetry row, KQL result, SecurityAlert, SecurityIncident. Stopping at KQL row match overstates confidence.

item.description:
CVE-2026-76581 (CVSS 9.8): Unauthenticated auth bypass in WPMU DEV Dashboard lets attackers claim an admin session on ~350,000 WordPress sites via HMAC canonicalization confusion in the Hub SSO flow. Patch to 5.0.2 now.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-76581, CVSS 9.8 Critical. Affects WPMU DEV Dashboard versions up to and including 5.0.1 on sites with Hub SSO enabled and mapped to an administrator. Exploitation is unauthenticated and leads to full site takeover, and to RCE if the plugin or theme editor is accessible.
- The root cause is HMAC canonicalization confusion between the two AJAX actions wdpsso_step1 and wdpsso_step2, both exposed to unauthenticated visitors. Step 1 signs token||state||redirect||domain without delimiters. Step 2 verifies token||state||redirect, omitting domain. item.title: Hunting Abuse: Detecting Privilege Escalation Through the ADCS Database
item.description:
The ADCS CA database is an underused forensic goldmine: it logs every certificate request including denied ones, exposing ESC1 privilege escalation attempts without any extra logging configuration.
Key findings:
- The CA database at C:\Windows\System32\CertLog\ is an ESE file that records all requests across four tables: Requests, Certificates, RequestAttributes, and inline request text. Denied requests are preserved permanently, meaning an attacker who tried and failed to impersonate a privileged identity via a misconfigured template still leaves a record including the UPN they specified as the Subject Alternative Name.
- CISA Advisory AA26-237A (August 2026) confirms ESC1 was used in red team assessments to compromise domains. ESC1 lets any domain user request a certificate for any other user when templates allow enrollee-supplied subjects and permit Client Authentication, producing a valid TGT for the impersonated account.
- A bug in the go-ese library caused all DateTime columns in the ADCS database to return 1899-12-30T00:00:00Z because Flags=0 columns were decoded as OLE doubles instead of Windows FILETIMEs. The fix, now merged and shipping in Velociraptor 0.76.6+, inspects the float value itself to select the correct decoder.

item.title: I’m in your logs now: deceiving analysts and blinding EDRs
item.description:
ETW telemetry can be spoofed, capped into blindness, or buffer-flooded from unelevated user mode, undermining EDR visibility without touching a kernel driver or requiring admin rights.
Key findings:
- From an unelevated user-mode process, a researcher registered existing ETW manifest-based providers (including Microsoft-Windows-LDAP-Client and Microsoft-Windows-Antimalware) and emitted structurally valid fake events. Because ETW has no strong per-emitter authentication, MDE's cloud pipeline accepted the synthetic telemetry as legitimate, producing fake SharpHound-style LDAP alerts and fake AV detections that real analysts responded to.
- MDE caps certain providers, for example the LDAP-Client provider hits a global per-machine ceiling (observed at 1,000 events in testing) that resets after roughly 24 hours. Once that cap is hit, all subsequent legitimate events for that period are silently dropped. An attacker can pre-flood the cap with noise before running the real operation; the malicious activity simply never appears in the cloud dataset.
- ETW real-time session buffer pools are shared across providers. If a consumer stops draining its buffer, the pool fills and the session controller instructs all connected providers to stop emitting, which can starve other consumers including the EDR. Windows also limits total active trace sessions to 64; exhausting that ceiling blocks new session creation entirely.
- MSRC received the report in January 2025.

item.title: Assembly for Malware Analysis
item.description:
A practical x86/x64 assembly reading guide for analysts: recover argument flow, identify API sequences, and reconstruct behavior without memorizing the full instruction set.
Key findings:
- Calling convention errors are the fastest path to misreading a function. Windows x64 passes args in RCX, RDX, R8, R9 with 32 bytes of shadow space; System V AMD64 uses RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9. Applying the wrong ABI to a sample silently breaks every argument label downstream.
- PEB walking via gs:[0x60] (x64) or fs:[0x30] (x86) without touching the IAT is a reliable indicator of dynamic API resolution in packers, reflective loaders, and shellcode. Treat sparse imports plus that pattern as a prompt to trace every GetProcAddress-equivalent call and its returned pointer.
- The worked example nails the analyst loop: a pre-write XOR transform (key 0x23) followed by WriteFile. The transform loop uses jae (unsigned), confirming the length is treated as unsigned. Identifying that before labeling behavior avoids the signed/unsigned misread listed explicitly as a common mistake.
- Indirect calls (call rax, call qword ptr [rip+offset]) demand source tracing every time. The target may be a resolved import, a virtual method, a callback, or a trampoline into freshly decoded memory. The allocation size, protection flags, and eventual control-transfer destination are the evidence that distinguishes them.

item.title: From SQL Injection to Remote Code Execution: Following an Unexpected Attack Chain
item.description:
Error-based SQL injection in a URL path segment escalated to authenticated RCE through upload bypass and WAF evasion, exposing shared-hosting tenants beyond the original target.
Key findings:
- SQLi lived in a numeric path segment (/details/{id}/...), not a query string, so automated scanners missed it. item.title: Threat Hunting using Pair Probabilities
item.description:
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint's pair_probabilities_fl() function can be adapted into a probabilistic threat hunt that surfaces binaries running from statistically unusual directories, without writing a single signature.
Key details:
- The KQL function pair_probabilities_ext_fl() takes two categorical columns (A and B) and calculates P_AIB (how rare is this directory for this binary?) and P_BIA (how rare is this binary for this directory?), plus Lift and Jaccard metrics. A low P_AIB on cmd.exe is what flags it running once from \users\user\desktop versus 133,607 times from \windows\system32.
- Path normalization is critical before feeding data in: user paths collapse to user, GUIDs to uuid, temp filenames to random.tmp, and drive letters are stripped. Without it, structural path variants inflate apparent rarity and flood results with noise.
- The hunt targets a curated list of living-off-the-land binaries including cmd.exe, powershell.exe, rundll32.exe, certutil.exe, mshta.exe, wmic.exe, and others. A second variant dynamically identifies Microsoft-signed binaries normally resident in System32 or SysWOW64, making the scope environment-driven rather than static.
- Key limitations: low observation counts make probabilities unreliable; if attacker behavior is already repetitive in your baseline window it blends in; and rarity is not malice, it is a triage signal only.

item.title: Inside Elastic's agentic SOC: How we took AI alert triage from 60% to 92% accuracy
item.description:
Elastic's agentic SOC pipeline jumped from 60% to 92% AI triage accuracy, not by swapping models, but by engineering the right context window before any verdict is made.
Key findings:
- The accuracy gap was a context problem, not a model problem. Agents working only on current alert data were wrong 40% of the time. Analysts stopped reading summaries entirely. The fix: pre-fetching the detection rule's investigation guide via GET /api/alerting/rule/<kibana.alert.rule.uuid>, user risk signals from Workday (new hires, departing employees, high-risk cost centers), and 30 days of closed cases for that same rule ID before the agent reasons at all.
- Three specialized agents replace one bloated agent. Pattern Finder ingests historical case records and returns structured JSON with FP rate, user risk flag, and severity recommendation. No tools, no external queries, no prompt injection risk. L1 Investigation Agent runs ES|QL queries and external enrichment, following the per-rule investigation guide as primary triage instructions. Summarizer formats the final Markdown output for cases and Slack, making no investigative decisions itself.
- The feedback loop is the key mechanism. Each case stores AI Verdict, AI Confidence, and an analyst-toggled "AI Incorrect" custom field. PastCasesbyRulenameLookup feeds those fields back into the next agent run so the Pattern Finder can detect its own overclassification errors before making a new call.
